newsitem.title: USA: U.S. foreign crudes thin amid robust Euro demand.
newsitem.headline: U.S. foreign crudes thin amid robust Euro demand.

text.p: U.S. foreign crudes were thin Monday amid robust demand in Europe, where a widespread cold snap is whipping up demand for heating oil, traders said.
"As soon as that weather breaks, Brent will be flooding over here," noted one Texas trader.
The spread between February West Texas Intermediate and North Sea Brent stood around $1.60 a barrel, a level which more than covers transatlantic shipping costs.
The notional price for Brent deliveries into the U.S. Gulf Coast is WTI minus 30 cents for February barrels, traders said.
IPE Brent crude ended firm Monday after a session marked by weather-related gains in the gas oil contract.
Severe cold temperatures throughout Europe spurred demand, particularly for gas oil in German.
Wet Brent traded at February Brent plus 15 cents for January 11-13, while one million barrels of Oseberg changed hands at Dated Brent plus 43 cents for January 16-18.
In Latin America, Bolivia's state-owned oil company sold a cargo of reconstituted crude to a Wall Street trader for loading January 6-10, trade sources said.

Yacimientos Petroliferos Fiscales Bolivianos (YPFB) sold the 300,000 barrel cargo to Argentina's Energy trading on behalf of Basis Petroleum, a unit of Salomon Brothers, for a discount of between $4.00 and $5.00 a barrel to WTI, traders said.
Elsewhere, Colombia's state-owned Ecopetrol is accepting bids tomorrow for a cargo of Cano Limon crude for loading mid-February, trade sources said.
In the U.S. aftermarket, a series of partial paper February Brent cargoes traded at $23.60 a barrel, down six cents from the IPE settlement.
Jan/Feb Brent changed hands at a steady 35 cents, while Feb/Mar Brent was dealt at 56 cents, up three cents from the IPE settlement.
